name: LLM & AI Security
description: Security and privacy of large language models and generative AI: prompt injection, jailbreaks, and LLM-assisted security.

uss.narrative:
USENIX Security's engagement with LLM and AI security began before large generative models dominated headlines. Early work focused on NLP-backed threat intelligence: Reading Thieves' Cant (USENIX 2018) showed automated NLP could interpret obfuscated criminal jargon on dark-web markets. As DNN-based text classifiers became deployment targets, T-Miner (USENIX 2021) proposed a generative defence against Trojan triggers embedded in those classifiers — one of the first USENIX papers treating an NLP model itself as an adversarial target. Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models via Linguistic Style Manipulation (USENIX 2022) then showed the attack side: linguistic style alone could serve as a stealthy backdoor trigger, raising the threat bar for any organization deploying fine-tuned language models.

The arrival of large generative models in 2023 produced an immediate wave of privacy and integrity research. Glaze (USENIX 2023) tackled a new harm — artists' visual style being mimicked by text-to-image models — and proposed perturbation-based protection that sparked significant real-world adoption. CodexLeaks (USENIX 2023) demonstrated that code-generation models like GitHub Copilot memorize and regurgitate private training data, establishing a template for LLM memorisation audits. Two-in-One (USENIX 2023) introduced the concept of model hijacking, repurposing a deployed text-generation model for an attacker's covert task, extending prior classification-model attack ideas to the generative setting.

By 2024, safety alignment and jailbreaking became the dominant research front. Making Them Ask and Answer (USENIX 2024) broke alignment in a small number of queries via a disguise-and-reconstruct technique; LLM-Fuzzer (USENIX 2024) turned classic fuzzing methodology into a scalable jailbreak template generator, demonstrating that safety evaluation is fundamentally a fuzzing problem. Instruction Backdoor Attacks Against Customized LLMs (USENIX 2024) moved beyond public models to attack the GPT-style customization layer, while Malla (USENIX 2024) measured the real underground economy of LLM-integrated criminal services. The What Was Your Prompt? attack (USENIX 2024) exposed a side-channel in encrypted AI-assistant traffic that could reconstruct users' queries from token-length patterns alone.

The 2025 cohort reflects maturation on both attack and defence fronts. JBShield (USENIX 2025) countered jailbreaks by analysing activated internal concepts to detect and neutralise disguised inputs at inference time. Research expanded into agent-level threats: Make Agent Defeat Agent (USENIX 2025) used one LLM agent to automatically surface taint-style vulnerabilities in another, and Cloak, Honey, Trap (USENIX 2025) developed proactive honeypot defences against autonomous LLM penetration-testing agents. RAG-specific attack vectors also emerged — PoisonedRAG and Topic-FlipRAG (USENIX 2025) showed that injecting crafted documents into a retrieval corpus could hijack or manipulate grounded LLM outputs, opening a new poisoning surface as RAG deployment spread.

ccs.narrative:
LLM and generative AI security emerged as a major CCS research area almost simultaneously with the public release of large foundation models. The 2023 cohort established the initial threat landscape across three domains. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) quantified the real-world risk of AI code generation. DE-FAKE: Detection and Attribution of Fake Images Generated by Text-to-Image Generation Models (CCS 2023) addressed synthetic media forensics. Unsafe Diffusion: On the Generation of Unsafe Images and Hateful Memes From Text-To-Image Models (CCS 2023) measured how diffusion models can be prompted to produce harmful content.

By 2024, jailbreaks and prompt injection became primary attack categories. "Do Anything Now": Characterizing and Evaluating In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts on Large Language Models (CCS 2024) systematically categorized jailbreak prompts collected from the wild, measuring their effectiveness across models. Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge (CCS 2024) showed that LLM-as-judge evaluation pipelines are manipulable via adversarial inputs. PLeak: Prompt Leaking Attacks against Large Language Model Applications (CCS 2024) demonstrated extraction of confidential system prompts.

Backdoor attacks against pre-trained models had been anticipated: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All (CCS 2021) showed that trojan backdoors survive fine-tuning in NLP, foreshadowing the LLM supply-chain threat. zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models (CCS 2024) closed the loop by enabling verifiable inference, providing a cryptographic foundation for trustworthy LLM deployment.

milestones.title: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All
milestones.note: Showed backdoors in pre-trained NLP models persist across any downstream fine-tuning, warning of LLM supply-chain risks.

milestones.note: Produced the first ZK proofs for correct LLM inference at scale, enabling trustworthy verifiable AI deployment.

ndss.narrative:
LLM and generative AI security appeared at NDSS first as an offshoot of earlier adversarial text work. TextBugger (NDSS 2019) demonstrated that character- and word-level perturbations can fool real-world text classification services, laying groundwork for later jailbreak and prompt injection research. The field lay relatively dormant at NDSS until the GPT era catalyzed a burst of papers from 2024 onward.

Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing (NDSS 2024) showed that LLMs can parse protocol specifications and guide fuzzing engines, achieving 281 citations quickly and signaling that LLMs as security tools were a major new direction. DeGPT (NDSS 2024) demonstrated that LLMs can improve decompiler output, turning reverse engineering into an LLM-assisted workflow. Both papers reflect an optimistic view of LLMs as force multipliers for defenders.

The 2025 cohort introduced a more adversarial perspective on LLMs as targets. I Know What You Asked: Prompt Leakage via KV-Cache Sharing in Multi-Tenant LLM Deployments (NDSS 2025) revealed a side-channel attack on shared inference infrastructure; Safety Misalignment Against Large Language Models (NDSS 2025) examined how models can be steered past safety constraints; and From Large to Mammoth (NDSS 2025) provided a comparative evaluation of LLMs for vulnerability discovery, beginning the process of benchmarking these tools with the rigor the security community expects.

milestones.title: TextBugger: Generating Adversarial Text Against Real-world Applications
milestones.note: TextBugger generates adversarial text perturbations that fool real-world deep-learning text classification and sentiment systems.

milestones.title: Interpretable Federated Transformer Log Learning for Cloud Threat Forensics
milestones.note: Uses interpretable federated transformer log learning for cloud threat detection and forensic analysis.

milestones.title: Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing
milestones.note: Uses an LLM to guide protocol fuzzing of implementations lacking machine-readable specifications.

milestones.title: DeGPT: Optimizing Decompiler Output with LLM
milestones.note: Uses an LLM to refine decompiler output, making reverse-engineered pseudocode more readable and comprehensible.

milestones.title: I Know What You Asked: Prompt Leakage via KV-Cache Sharing in Multi-Tenant LLM Serving
milestones.note: Shows shared KV-cache in multi-tenant LLM serving leaks other users' prompts.

milestones.title: From Large to Mammoth: A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models in Vulnerability Detection
milestones.note: Comparatively evaluates large language models on software vulnerability detection performance.

milestones.title: Safety Misalignment Against Large Language Models
milestones.note: Evaluates robustness of LLM safety alignment against diverse malicious attacks that induce unsafe content.

milestones.title: Beyond Classification: Inferring Function Names in Stripped Binaries via Domain Adapted LLMs
milestones.note: Uses domain-adapted LLMs to infer function names in stripped binaries for malware and vulnerability analysis.

sp.narrative:
LLM security at IEEE S&P began before the GPT era, with early papers on language-model privacy and NLP adversarial attacks. Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models (S&P 2020) demonstrated that models trained on sensitive corpora memorize and reproduce private information. Adversarial Watermarking Transformer: Towards Tracing Text Provenance with Data Hiding (S&P 2021) addressed the complementary challenge of detecting whether text was AI-generated.

The 2022 cohort mapped the adversarial-NLP landscape. Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks (S&P 2022) showed that homoglyph and invisible-character perturbations fool NLP classifiers invisibly. Spinning Language Models: Risks of Propaganda-As-A-Service (S&P 2022) demonstrated that fine-tuning or output manipulation could turn models into propaganda generators. Piccolo: Exposing Complex Backdoors in NLP Transformer Models (S&P 2022) found complex multi-token trigger patterns in transformer backdoors.

2023 marked the GPT moment for S&P. Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models (S&P 2023) showed that large foundation models memorize PII at alarming rates. Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models (S&P 2023) found LLMs can sometimes patch security bugs but are inconsistent. Deepfake Text Detection: Limitations and Opportunities (S&P 2023) characterized the arms race between generation and detection.

By 2024-2025, jailbreaking and prompt injection dominated. SneakyPrompt: Jailbreaking Text-to-image Generative Models (S&P 2024) developed adversarial prompts that bypass safety filters. DataSentinel: A Game-Theoretic Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks (S&P 2025) addressed the emergent prompt-injection threat in deployed LLM agents, reflecting the field's rapid pivot from studying models to securing deployed LLM-powered systems.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this area treated language models less as assistants and more as text classifiers and generators to be attacked or probed. Around 2018-2019 the focus was adversarial text and underground language: "Reading Thieves' Cant" (USENIX 2018) mined obfuscated jargon from cybercrime forums, while "TextBugger" (NDSS 2019) showed that small, often imperceptible perturbations could fool real-world NLP services. As pretrained transformers arrived, the threat surface shifted toward the models themselves — "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020) demonstrated that embeddings from BERT and GPT-2 leak sensitive attributes, and a wave of CCS/USENIX/S&P papers in 2021-2022 mapped out training-time threats: backdoors that transfer across tasks ("Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All", CCS 2021), stealthy linguistic-style triggers ("Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack", USENIX 2022), and defenses/detectors like "T-Miner" (USENIX 2021) and "Piccolo" (S&P 2022). "Bad Characters" (S&P 2022) extended imperceptible attacks to the encoding level.

The 2023 cohort marks the pivot to generative AI as a deployed product. On the privacy side, "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) showed real PII extraction from LMs. A large cluster turned to text-to-image systems: "Glaze" (USENIX 2023) and later "Nightshade" (S&P 2024) gave artists poisoning-based defenses against style mimicry, while "Unsafe Diffusion" and "DE-FAKE" (both CCS 2023) studied harmful generation and provenance. Crucially, the community also began studying LLMs as security tools and as risks to their users — "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" (CCS 2023) and "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair" (S&P 2023) framed the dual-use question of code assistants.

By 2024 the defining threats became prompt injection and jailbreaks at internet scale. "Do Anything Now" (CCS 2024) was a landmark empirical study of in-the-wild jailbreak prompts, complemented by automated attack machinery like "LLM-Fuzzer" (USENIX 2024) and "Making Them Ask and Answer" (USENIX 2024). Prompt injection matured from anecdote to formalized attack with "PLeak" prompt-leaking and "Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge" (both CCS 2024), while "Instruction Backdoor Attacks Against Customized LLMs" (USENIX 2024) showed the GPTs ecosystem inherits backdoor risk. In parallel, LLMs proved genuinely useful for offense and defense — "LLM guided Protocol Fuzzing" (NDSS 2024), "PentestGPT" (USENIX 2024), and "DeGPT" (NDSS 2024) — even as "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities" (S&P 2024) tempered the hype.

The current frontier (2024-2025) is defense and verification. "SecAlign" (CCS 2025) hardens models against prompt injection via preference optimization and "DataSentinel" (S&P 2025) brings a game-theoretic detector, signaling a shift from cataloging attacks to building principled, evaluable defenses. Cryptographic guarantees are entering too, with "zkLLM" (CCS 2024) offering zero-knowledge proofs over model inference and "AirGapAgent" (CCS 2024) enforcing contextual privacy for conversational agents. The arc runs from perturbing text classifiers, through poisoning and backdooring pretrained models, to today's twin agenda: defending deployed generative systems against injection/jailbreaks while harnessing the same models as security tooling.
